title: Visiting Venuti's wartime band in Miami
summary: During wartime shortages Venuti hired two girl saxophonists from the union and laughed through their poor playing; Challis explains his hiring problems with 4-F musicians.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Well, Spike said, he said, "Hey, what do you say we go over to the place, the joint and see Joe and get some laughs?"

So we went over there, the dances ran there. There was this service place, the Air Force place, where all the guys, the enlisted men were there, and draftees and they'd come dancing in this place, and it started at 8 o'clock and finished off at 12:00. No real late stuff there.

So we went over, we got over there a little early while they were setting up. quarter of eight maybe, and we talked to Joe and during those times, everybody was having trouble with your musicians, they are all 4-F's.

He was having his troubles and we are having ours. And I had charge of hiring them, you see, I couldn't fire them, but I could hire them. And boy I got to try hard not to make a mistake, because there was some real kooks that you'd pick up that they got out of some other band and they were only around because they were 4-F. They would get out and you would try to get the dope on them. "Oh, they play good, but -- and you never knew what the but was so you got them in the band.
And then they'd wind up with tea, smoking tea or

Anyway we went over and there's Joe, we talked to Joe, he had a couple guys there that we knew, and we gabbed and talked about the business and how it was and he was having his problems. He says he's now without two saxophones players.

He said, "I called up the union this afternoon and asked them to send me two saxophone players to come to the job by 8 o'clock." Well, they hadn't shown up. So they're all tuning up, getting straightened out, getting set up and looked down the door, and in come a couple with saxophones under their arm with -- the way I used to carry mine, with felt, the green felt. They got them under their arms and they come in, and it's a couple of girls.

They come down, hiya, and so forth, and so on, and Joe says, "Sit here, sit here, take this book, take that book." Fine, all right to them. So there's hardly anybody there so they ran over a couple of numbers and he said, "Take one," and the girl takes one and it wasn't bad. I mean, it wasn't good, awful. So Joe's laughing, "Great, great, take another." And he went on like that, and Spike and I had a fit, but we could tell with Joe, he could put up with something like that. It could be rotten, lousy and he'd put up with it and make a joke out of it.
I don't know what the rest of them thought, but it

was really something, and he had the other one do the same thing. We got out of there very shortly, after we said hello and listened to a couple of numbers. But to see these girls come in and have them set and happened right off, give them a chorus, to take, He wanted to hear everything they could do and it was pretty bad. "Take another."
